ORAL   ANSWERS   TO   QUESTIONS 
Cut in CNG supply to industrial units 
*581. SHRI  RAJEEV SHUKLA: Will the Minister of  PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Compressed Natural Gas supply to many 
Idustrial houses has been cut to meet its increased demand in Delhi; 
(b) if so, the loss of production of industrial units with depleted CNG 
apply; 
 
(c) by when the Indraprastha Gas Ltd. (I.G.L.) will be able to meet the full 
squirement of Delhi; and 
(d) the steps taken to increase the supply of Compressed Natural Gas to 
idustrial units? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on theTable of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d)To meet the current Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) requirement 
of public transport in Delhi 50 per cent  of the fall back allocation to M/s 
Maruti Udyog Limited (MUL), which was meant for captive power generation, 
was reduced. Since dual fuel facilities are available with M/s MUL for captive 
power generation, the question of loss of production does not arise. To bridge 
the gap between the demand and supply of natural gas, steps such as import of 
liquefied natural gas and speeding up of indigenous exploration/exploitation 
of domestic hydrocarbon resources have been initiated. Indraprastha Gas 
Limited plans to meet the requirement of Delhi during the year 2003-04.

Department. And, Sir, as the hon. Member is aware, there is a procedure; income-tax is a

assessment will be issued, then the assessee has the alternative of either paying the 
tax or disputing it before the appellate authorities; if he disputes it before the 
appellate authorities, as we have found in some cases, then the prescribed legal 
procedure takes its course. Now, we cannot short-circuit that prescribed legal 
procedure. And, therefore, this impression, Sir, that we are not being pro-active, is

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDY): (a) The organic tea was introduced 
to the world market in th e mid 1980s. Over the past  decade, its consumption 
has grown by more than 10% per year globally. However, in volume terms, the 
trading in organic tea is very insignif icant when compared to the black tea. 
India is the leading producer of both non organic as well as organic tea in the 
world, the entire Indian production of organic tea is exported. The major 
destinations are UK, Germany, USA and Japan. The other major organic tea

4293. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have received any representation from the Indian 
Cotton Mills Federation, New Delhi regarding rationalisation of excise duty 
for textile industry; 
(b) if so, the details of issues raised in their representation thereof; 
(c) whether Government have taken up this representation for active 
consideration; 
(d) if so, what is the Government's reaction thereto; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor and by when action is likely to be taken in 
the matter? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) and (b) The Indian Cotton Mills 
Federation (ICMF) had sent pre-budget representations regarding rationalisation 
of excise duty for textile fabrics. The issues raised by them included completion 
of the CENVAT chain covering all stages of manufacture from fibres to garments, 
allowing of the CENVAT credit at the processed fabric stage of actuals basis and 
discontinuing the system of deemed CENVAT credit,  withdrawal of excise 
exemptions of hank yam, hand processed textile fabrics when power is used for 
specified finishing processes, knitwear s and readymade garm ents in the SSI 
sector, abolition of optional stentor duty for independent textile processors 
and rationalization of excise duty structure on fibres and yarns, fabrics, made-
up and ready-made garments. 
100 

[7 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) and (d) The Government have considered all the representations 
received from the textile industry including that from ICMF in the budget and 
have announced a special package of incentives for the textile industry. These 
include reduction of excise duty on fabrics, made-ups and garments from 16% to 
12%, withdrawal of excise exemption on hank yam, restricting the exemption 
on hand processed fabrics on use of power to 7/4 specified processes, levy of 
excise duty on optional basis on grey fabrics, cotton knitted fabrics and knitwears, 
abolition of optional compounded levy scheme for independent textile 
processors and exemption from excise duty on automatic looms and specified 
textile processing machinery. 
(e) Does not arise in view of reply to parts (c) and (d) above.

4297. SHRI LAJPAT RAI: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state:

years for repatriation of sale proceeds by NRIs/PIOs; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefore; and

behalf for the next three years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) and (b) In terms of Regulation 6 of RBI's 
Notification No. 21/2000/RB dated May 3, 2000, NRIs and PIOs, have been permitted 
to repatriate sale proceeds of immovable property subject to certain conditions, inter-
alia, that the property is sold after 3 years from the date of acquisition or from the date 
of payment of final instalment whichever is later. As a result NRIs/PIOs who have-
entered into contracts to purchase properties in India are unable to take back their 
money unless they have paid full amount of purchase in the circumstances even in the 
cases where construction work is not progressing satisfactorily or for some compelling 
reasons the buyer has to cancel the contract, the funds brought in by the NRIs are 
blocked in India. In order to mitigate the difficulties faced by NRIs/PIOs Reserve Bank 
has decided henceforth to allow repatriation of sale proceeds or amount received on 
account of cancellation of purchase contracts, subject to the condition that the amount 
does not exceed amount paid for acquisition of the property in foreign exchange brought 
through Banking Channel or the amount realized whichever is lesser.

4302. SHRI SURESH KALMAD1: 
SHR1MATI AMBIKA SONI: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken any special measures to curb corruption 
in view of the arrest of some senior officials among the cadres of Indian Revenue 
Services; 
(b) if so, what type of a system of reward and punishment has been 
considered; 
(c) whether a system of objective cr iteria for transfers, postings and 
deputations has been considered; and

senior to Deputy Commissioners eligible for Cash Rewards so that they are not 
lured by unfair money? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) Government has taken several steps to 
check corruption, which include strengthening of the vigilance set up, closer 
monitoring by the Supervisory officers, use of information technology with a 
view to reducing the interface with the public, posting officers of integrity and 
efficiency in vigilance organizations, not giving sensitive postings to officers of 
doubtful integrity, keeping watch on the life-style of officers, drawing up of

level of Additional Commissioner in the Income Tax Department, and upto the

Indian Revenue Service, who are faci ng corruption charges, are generally 
transferred and posted to non-sensitive charges and are also not selected for 
deputation postings and for trainings.

Commissioner are already entitled to rewards. There is no proposal to grant

NPAs of Public Sector vis-a-vis Foreign Banks 
4305. SHRI NARENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the ratio of net Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) 
of Public Sector Banks is 2.26 per cent of total assets but in case of foreign binks 
it is only 0.79 per cent; 
(b) if so, whether this vast difference is attributable to management of the 
PSBs vis-a-vis foreign banks or whether there are any other reasons for this; and 
(c) whether any study has been made for recovery of NPAs during the last 
three years and whether any changes are required to improve the recovery of 
NPAs? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) and (b) The ratio of net NPAs to total assets of 
Public Sector Banks (PSBs) as on March 31,2001 was 2.72% and 0.8% for Foreign 
Banks. The major reasons for difference in ratio of net NPAs to total assets of 
PSBs and foreign banks is that the foreign banks operating in selected locations 
lend to selected clientele in selected areas with priority sector lending limited to 
export credit and credit to  SSI Sector. The PSBs with large rural network are 
required to lend to all sections of the society including agriculture, education, 
housing, Government sponsored schemes, weaker sections and other priority 
sectors as well. 
(c) Government and Reserve Bank of India (RBI) reviews the position of 
NPAs on a continuing basis and various measures have been taken for recovery 
of NPAs such as evolving and implementation of recovery policy by banks for 
110 

 
[7 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
restructuring, reschedutement and compromise settlement, filing of suits in DRTs 
and Courts, vigorous monitoring, supervision and follow up of Non-Performing 
Assets (NPAs) at various levels by the management. Further, Corporate Debt 
Restructuring mechanism has been put in place. Action has also been taken for 
setting up of Asset Reconstruction Companies. Legislative changes are proposed 
to facilitate securitisation, foreclosures and enforcement of securities in cases 
of default with the intervention of the Court. 
NABARD guidelines for rural banks 
4306. SHRI C. P.THTRUNAVUKKARASU: Will the Minister of 
FINANCE be pleased to state. 
(a) whether NABARD has issued guidelines to improve functioning of 
Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks in the States; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the NABARD has examined the problem faced by Cooperative 
Agriculture and Rural Development Banks in various States; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) the measures proposed to be taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) and (b) National Bank for Agriculture and 
Rural Development (NABARD) has reported that it has issued guidelines and 
taken a number of initiatives for improving the working of the State Cooperative 
Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (SCARDBs). These measures include 
preparation of institution-specific development action plans (DAPs) aimed at 
attaining current/sustainable viability in the shortest possible time-frame and 
implementation and monitoring the same through the mechanism of Memorandum 
of Understanding (MoU). These guidelines were revised in July, 2000 for 
incorporating implementation of prudential norms (income recognition, asset 
classification and provisioning norms), etc. Guidelines were further issued in 
April,2001 for implementing one-time stetement scheme (OTS) to reduce the 
level of non- performing assets. 
(c) to (e) Government had set up a task Force to stud y the cooperative 
credit system and suggest measures for its strengthening under the Chairmanship 
of Shri Jagdish Capoor. The Task Force found that SCARDBs were suffering 
111 

RAJYA SABHA [7 May, 2002] 
from duality of control, lack of professional management, high intermediation 
cost, low profitability/losses, poor recovery, high levels of non-performing 
assets, etc. The Task Force recommende d a four dimensional revitalization 
package encompassing financial, operational, organization and systematic 
aspects including recapitalisation of po tentially viable cooperative credit 
institutions. Subsequently, a committee under the Chairmanship of Minister of 
State for Finance had been constituted for consideration of revitalization 
assistance to cooperative banks. Subsequent to the submission of the report by 
the Committee, Government has made a provision of Rs. 100 crore in the 
Budget for the year 2002-2003 for revitalising the cooperative banks including 
Agriculture and Rural Development Banks.

Working capital for small scale sector 
4327. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether the Confederation of Indian Industries has inter alia suggested 
Government to have a sub target within priority sector lending to promote 
alternative sources of finance, to establish an independent credit rating agency 
and to make the Nayak Committee norms regarding working capital applicable 
131 

RAJYA  SABHA               [7 May, 2002] 
as a rule to alleviate the capital related problems of small scale industry; 
(b) if so, whether Government have examined these suggestion; and 
(c) if so, what is Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) yes, sir. 
(b) and (c) Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has reported that no sub-target has 
been prescribed for financing SSI Units within the priority sector lending targets. 
According to RBI, the public sector banks advances to SSI Units have shown 
steady increase in absolute terms and that even without any target, out of 40% of 
target for priority sectors, agriculture and SSI together account for 34 percentage points, 
thus leaving only 6% for the rest of other important segments of priority sectors such 
small business, retail trade, housing, education and self-employed person etc. Fixing 
sub target may result in crowding out in other priority sectors, RBI has, therefore, 
decided not to fix any sub-target for SSI within the priority sector lending. Banks 
are however being advised by RBI to fix a target for the year on year growth in 
SSI. 
As regards computation of working capital limits for SSI, Banks are 
reportedly computing the same on the basis of minimum 20% of the annual 
projected turn over upto a borrowal limit of Rs. 5 crore as per Nayak Committee 
recommendations. RBI's Study of specialized SSI and General Branches revealed that 
working capital was computed on the basis of the norms in 93% of the proposals 
received in specialized SSI Branches and about 79 percent of proposals received in 
general branches.

Impact of EEZ on Crude Production 
4335. SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU): Will the Minister of 
PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether all off-shore installations of the ONGC and other oil 
exploration companies engaged in off-shore explorations would be treated as part of 
Domestic Tariff Area (DTA), as a result of the recent Government decision to bring the 
entire Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and continental shelf under the jurisdiction of 
the Customs Act, 1962; and 
(b) if so, in what manner this will affect the cost structure of the crude 
production of ONGC and others engaged in off-shore exploration; and how the cost of 
production of crude by them would compare with international crude production? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS (SHRI SANTOSH GANGWAR): (a) Yes, Sir. The Government has issued 
a Notification No. 157 on 7.2.02 under clause (a) of Sub-section (6) of Section 6 and 
clause (a) of sub-section (7) of Section 7 of the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, 
Exclusive Economic Zone and other Maritime Zones Act, 1976 (80 of 1976) extending 
the Customs Act, 1962 and Customs Tariff Act, 1975 to the continental shelf and the 
exclusive economic zone of India with effect from the date of publication of the 
notification in the Official Gazette i.e. 11.2.2002. 
(b) The cost of production of crude oil and natural gas depends amongst other 
factors on the fiscal regime, comprising royalty, customs duty etc. In the offshore areas, 
while Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. (ONGC) is liable to pay the applicable 
customs duty on procurements for its ar eas allotted on nomination basis, no 
customs duty is payable on procurements by the 
145 

 
RAJYA SABHA [7 May, 2002] 
Contractors under the Production Sharing Contracts for exploration blocks 
and discovered fields. Customs duty is a dynamic factor and its impact on 
ONGC's costing cannot be assessed in advance. The operating cost of producing 
crude oil and natural gas by Indian companies, including ONGC, is comparable 
with international costs in this regard.

Policy on inter-State water sharing 
4372. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned "Water policy silent on Inter-State sharing" which appeared in 'The 
Hindu' dated the 2nd April, 2002; 
(b) if so, whether the revised policy is silent on inter-State water sharing 
which has been referred to the National Water Board; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the steps taken to implement the policy in consultation with all the 
State Governments? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. 
The National Water Resources Council, while adopting the revised National 
Water Policy, 2002 in its 5th meeting held on 1st April, 2002, decided to refer 
the "National Policy Guidelines for Water Allocation amongst States" to the 
National Water Board for arriving at consensus on these guidelines. 
However, the National Water Policy, 2002 adopted by the National Water 
Resources Council has a provision in its para 21.1 regarding inter-State water 
sharing which envisages that "The water sharing/distribution amongst the 
States should be guided by a national perspective with due regard to water 
resources availability and needs within the river basin. Necessary guidelines, 
including for water short States even outside the basin, need to be evolved for 
facilitating future agreements amongst the basin States." 
The policy, inter-alia, envisages that each State should formulate its own 
State Water-Policy backed with an ope rational action plan in a time-bound 
manner within a period of two years and implement the same in order to achieve 
the desired objectives as laid down in the Policy.

RAJYA SABHA [7 May, 2002] 
Scheme to integrate rivers 
† 4374. SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are formulating any scheme to integrate the 
rivers of the country and conservation of their water in order to escape from the 
calamity like floods; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the steps being taken by Government to save Bihar from the losses 
caused by floods of water coming from Nepal every year; 
(d) whether Government have talked with the Government of Nepal in 
this regard; and 
 (e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) In 1980, the Ministry of Water Resources, then known as the Ministry 
of Irrigation, formulated a National Perspective Plan for integrated water resources 
development through inter-linkages of several southern based Peninsular rivers 
and the Himalayan rivers which inter alia envisages flood control benefit. The 
National Water Development Agency (NWDA) established by the Government 
of-India in 1982 to inter-alia canrryout water balance and feasibility studies has 
identified 30 Links under National Perspective for preparation of Feasibility Report 
and has completed Feasibility Report of 6 links. 
(c) to (e) Flood Management being a State subject, flood control schemes 
are planned, funded and executed by the State Governments themselves out of 
their own resources and as per their own priorities. The Central Government 
renders assistance that are technical, catalytical and promotional in nature. 
† Origirial notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
176 

[7 May, 2002] RAJYASABHA 
As a non-structural measure of flood management, a scheme namely, 
"Flood forecasting & Warning System on rivers common to India and Nepal" is 
in operation since 1989 for exchange of hydrological and meteorological data 
from Nepal to India for flood forecasts. 
Further the discussions have been conducted with Nepal on minimizing 
the effects of floods from rivers originating from Nepal in this regard a joint 
Inception Report has been finalised for Sapra Koshi High Dam Multipurpose 
Project and Sun Kosi Storage cum-diversion Scheme paving the way for setting 
up of Joint Project Officer and preparation of Joint Detailed Project Report 
having inter-alia flood control benefits for Bihar. 
In additon, in order to prevent spilling of flood waters from Lalbakeya, 
Bagmati, Khando and Kamla rivers from Nepal side into Bihar, both sides have 
agreed to extend the embankments in no man's land and work on Lalbakeya is 
nearing completion. 
For dealing with the pr oblems of inundation in the vicinity of India-
Nepal border, a Standing Committee on Inundation Problems between India 
and Nepal is also functioning since 1986. So far, twelve meetings have been 
held in which various issues have been sorted out. Apart from this, the 
Government of India has set up High Level Committees on Kosi and Gandak 
rivers to inspect and recommend measures to protect the banks of the two rivers 
in and around Kosi and Gandak barrages from erosion. 
In order to have inter-action at higher level, a Joint Committee on Water 
Resources headed by the respective Wate r Resources Secretaries of both the 
countries has also been established to oversee the entire gamut of India-Nepal 
co-operation in the Water Resources Sector. 
Recently, during March,2002, Prime Ministers of India and Nepal met in 
Delhi and amongst many other issues, matters concerning cooperation in the 
field of water resources were discussed which included matters to mitigate the 
adverse affects of floods from rivers flowing from Nepal.

DISCUSSION ON THE WORKING OF THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS 
SHRI K. NATWAR SINGH (Rajasthan): Mr. Chairman, Sir, when I 
joined the Indian Foreign Service 49 years ago, diplomats were told that a 
good diplomat thinks twice before saying nothing. In the past 50 years, the 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [7 May. 2002] 
content of diplomacy, the nature of diplomacy has altered the world over. In 
our country, for the past 50 years, t here has been a broad national consensus 
on the foreign policy. The framework that  Nehru constructed has survived the 
test of the time even when some super ficial and supercilious predators have 
tried to tamper with that framework. You abandon Nehru and you are left 
naked in the foreign affairs field. 
I will begin by mentioning the important link between the domestic 
policy and the foreign policy. This is mo st dramatically made available to the 
country and to the House by the recent  events in Gujarat. I will quote from a 
book written by P.N. Haksar whom the Mi nister of External Affairs, like me, 
admires very much. Nehruji said, "Foreign policies depend ultimately on 
internal conditions and developments. In ternal progress for us, therefore, 
becomes essential if we have to play an effective part in world affairs". Shri 
P.N. Haksar says, "Thus sovereignty and independence are indispensable to 
conduct of foreign policy of any nation and even if a country is sovereign and 
independent, it cannot effectively pursue a foreign policy unless it is cohesive 
within itself and consistent in its purpose." 
I have been a representativ e of India for 31 years and it has been a 
great honour to me because India has on e of the best Foreign Services in the 
world. We come to the Foreign Servic es through one of the most difficult 
competitive examinations that the world has to offer. But the instrument that 
the diplomats have to have is a clear-c ut policy framework and a leadership 
which is familiar with the foundations of India's foreign policy laid down before 
Independence; what are its sources of in spirations and what are the springs 
from which it flows. If you are not familia r with those, then you fall into the kind 
of traps we have been falling for the la st few years. One of the fundamental 
problems that the present dispensation is confronted with is they are not clear 
about what India's foreign policy is. I say this with very great respect because I 
have respect for the shrines of the minds of all the Members in this House. For 
example, take the statement made by the Prime Minister in Ahmedabad before 
going to Singapore. Sir, 120 foreign missions in Delhi reported to their 
Governments that the Prime Minister of  India has spoken like a statesman. He 
comes back and speaks in Goa. The same 120 missions send reports to their 
Governments that the Prime Minister of India has spoken like a Swayam 
Sewak. Now the Prime Minister has been facing a great dilemma ever since he 
became Prime Minister.    When is he a statesman and when is he a 
198 

[7 May. 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
Swayam Sewak? Now it is no use telling the diplomats from this country or 
that country that you have no business to interfere in our internal affairs. The 
fact of the matter is that  a large number of people of Indian region are citttens 
of the USA, the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Netherlands. 
When their Governments, High Commissioners, Ambassadors, say, 
"Our citizens, who vote for us, have relations with Gujarat", they are 
concerned about their welfare. Then, how can you fault those Missions? I 
would have done the same thing if I was an Ambassador of this country. Sir, I 
have been in this game for nearly 50 years;  I am still learning. I am not sure if 
the dispensation in the External Affairs Ministry is aware of the shortcomings 
from which some of them suffer. 
Let me now come to the fundamental s of India's foreign policy, that 
is, non-alignment. It has become fashionable to say that non-alignment is not 
relevant. And I have seldom heard Jaswant Singhji resorting to any reference 
to non-alignment. He has done so rarely, and I would like him to read the 
Prime Minister's speech in Durban, wh ere the Prime Minister praised non-
alignment. "The Cold War has ended, the Warsaw Pact is wound up, but 
NATO is expanding to the borders of Russia." Against whom? If non-
alignment is irrelevant, then, I think, NATO is even more irrelevant? But I will 
tell you how and why non-alignment is rele vant even today as it was 20 years 
or 40 years, ago. The international age nda has changed, which, of course, is 
inevitable. When I represented India in  the 50's and the 60's, the agenda was 
colonialism, imperialism, rationalism, a partheid and so on. Today, the agenda 
is environment, drugs, AIDS, population and ecology. So, in this arena-ll, it 
would help us if the non-aligned movement had a proper leadership, and India 
is a country which can give that leadership, which this Government is not 
giving. But, on these issues which affect the human kind, we should take a 
lead in the non-aligned movement and speak with one voice. Let me quote 
from a very distinguished European St atesman, Dr. Richard von Weizsacker, 
who was the President of Germany for 10 years. In the lecture which he 
delivered at the Nehru Memorial in 2000, he said, "Nehru was among the first 
and foremost to look for a non-bloc internationalism. His idea of non-alignment 
became of global importance. He spoke about peace clubs against Cold War-
clubs, nuclear clubs. He was pondering how to create a sort of no-war-zone 
between the military blocs. From the outset his thoughts became and 
remained fruitful. Non-alignment was aiming at more than equidistance from 
blocs.   It was a denial of the gist of bloc thinking, an endeavour to 
199

SHRI T.N. CHATURVEDI (Uttar Pradesh): Thank you, Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir. I would like to say, at the very outset, that the Indian foreign 
policy is a positive one. It is a forward-looking one. It takes into account the 
changing circumstances and it believe s that there is a need for consensus 
within the country. The foreign policy of India emerged, as has been 
mentioned by Mr. Mukherjee, through the freedom struggle and the number of 
postulates that arose therefrom. There is no question of any deviation. So far 
as this Government is concerned, it has  only tried to build on it. It has only 
tried to shift the focus as called for by the circumstances. And that is why there 
is a needless apprehension and fear that there is an attempt to disown the 
legacy of Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru or somebody else. I do not know why my 
friend, Shri Natwar Singh, harbours such illusions? I cannot compete with him 
either in his experience in diplomacy or in his scholarship or the years that he 
has spent in a very useful service, by representing the country. 
Probably, many of the th ings that he has asked, would be replied to 
by the hon. Foreign Minister, as may be called for. But I was a little bit 
surprised by the barrage of vituperation that he unleashed, always, of course, 
referring to the hon. Foreign Minister. He said that diplomacy is how to do a 
thing, and foreign policy is what ought to be done. I think Shri Natwar Singh is 
not satisfied with being the Chairman of the Foreign Policy Group or Cell of his 
party. He is fumbling. He does not know what is to be done, and how to do it. 
He thinks that one way is, just try to start some kind of a posture of aggression 
that, probably, will demolish the Foreig n Minister, the foreign policy of the 
Government, and the Government itself. This is only in continuation of two 
simple things. I don't want to go into them. I just want to point out some 
positive features. The worry is Gujarat. Gujarat is again being brought in. I 
agree with my distinguished friend, Shri  Natwar Singh, that so far as the 
foreign policy is concerned, it hinges on the economic strengt h of country, on 
the social cohesion of the country, and how far we can speak and articulate 
our interests in one voice,
